title: AstraHealth VPC & On‑Prem Inference Runbook — Draft
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working briefing for AstraHealth Systems’ private inference deployment (hybrid VPC + on‑prem GPU cluster). The document captures sizing rationale, architecture assumptions, Terraform module guidance, upgrade/cutover strategy, and a prioritized set of open questions. Aim is to produce an operationally minimal, compliant environment for patient-facing inference APIs (FHIR/HL7 integration) with predictable latency and strong data isolation.

Goals & success criteria:
- Low-latency inference for triage workflows: 95th percentile tail latency <= 150ms for single-turn prompt (token window ~512).
- Scalable throughput: sustain 250 concurrent sessions (avg 60 tokens/s per session) with headroom for 2x burst.
- Data residency and auditability: all PHI-contained payloads must never leave customer VPC or on‑prem cluster; audit logs shipped to AstraHealth SIEM.
- Key management: keys managed by customer HSM via KMIP or BYOK KMS integration; Redwood control plane only receives metadata.

Customer constraints we must respect:
- Network: customer firewall allows egress only to specific Redwood control-plane endpoints via mutual TLS; some sites are air-gapped (no egress) and require packaged bundles.
- Hardware: primary rack uses NVIDIA H100S (80GB), secondary racks may be A100 40GB; procurement timeline for more H100s ~Q2 2026.
- Compliance: HIPAA + internal SOC-like policy; all metadata traces must have configurable redaction.
- Integration: AstraHealth uses FHIR R4 server for patient data; inference service will receive pre-sanitized features from backend, but must support on-demand PII redaction hooks.

Core proposal (high-level):
1) Hybrid topology: dedicated VPC peering to Redwood control plane (management only) + on‑prem inference pods behind customer NAT. For fully air-gapped sites, deliver a signed artifacts tarball + operator (k8s operator + systemd service) that runs inference runtime locally with local telemetry stashing.
2) Two-tier model deployment: primary H100 pool for low-latency, single-token-critical paths; lower-cost A100 pool for background batch/embedding jobs and retries. Automatic routing policy based on request profile.
3) Storage: NFS for model artifacts (readonly mounts) + local NVMe per node for KV cache and temp checkpoints. Models stored encrypted at rest with customer KMS wrapping.

Sizing rationale (back-of-envelope -> recommended initial config):
- Performance baseline: model = open-llm-family large (approx 10B dense / optimized for 8-bit). Measured single-token throughput on H100-80: ~120 tokens/sec per GPU under small-batch (1-4). For 250 concurrent sessions at 60 tokens/s => steady tokens/s = 15k.
- H100 pool sizing: 15,000 tokens/s / 120 tokens/s per GPU = ~125 GPUs. Add 25% headroom => 160 GPUs.
- A100 fallback pool: for background/queued tasks estimate 40 GPUs initial.
- Nodes: prefer 8x GPU multi-GPU servers (DGX-style) or 4x GPU blade racks depending on L2 network fabric. With 8x per node, 160 GPUs => 20 nodes. Plan initial cluster of 24 nodes (20 primary + 4 spare) to support maintenance and rolling upgrades.
- Networking: 100GbE leaf-spine inside cluster; BGP peering to customer edge. Public/private subnets per standard VPC design.
- Storage: Model storage 10TB replicated; NVMe 4TB per node for KV cache.

Terraform/module notes (practical guidance):
- Module layout: modules/networking, modules/compute, modules/kms-integration, modules/ops-agent, modules/autoscaler, modules/secrets-backend, modules/monitoring. Keep modules small and idempotent.
- Remote state: use customer-owned S3 backend with encryption and MFA delete enabled. State policy: per-environment workspaces (dev/staging/prod).
- Variables: expose knobs for gpu_type, gpu_count, node_size, network_cidr, kms_endpoint, audit_sink. Avoid embedding secrets in tfvars — reference secret manager only.
- Lifecycle rules: for model artifacts, treat model resource as a separate immutable resource (versioned object) so Terraform plans don't try to re-write model content on each run.
- Rolling update pattern: use a compute module with create_before_destroy=false and an in-place update with a small max_unavailable percentage (default 10%). Provide an explicit canary group tag to allow targeted canary updates.
- Air-gapped packaging: add a module/target that produces an offline bundle (.tar.gz + signed manifest) and a focus on reproducible builds: terraform output should include an artifact manifest referencing SHA256 checks.

Upgrade & cutover strategy (stepwise):
1) Preparation: validate Terraform plan in staging with identical node counts using synthetic workload harness. Run perf tests for latency and tail.
2) Canary (green path): deploy a 2-node canary group exposed to 3% traffic via routing rule. Monitor latency, error rates, model quality (sampled eval). Minimum stable window: 4 hours at normal load.
3) Phased ramp: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% over multiple maintenance windows; keep fallback routing to A100 pool if latency or error threshold breached.
4) Post-cutover validation: run regression evals tied to AstraHealth prompt suite (20 prompts) and compare embeddings similarity metrics; verify audit logs and KMS key usage events.
5) Rollback: maintain imagemap of previous runtime + explicit terraform workspace snapshot. Rolling rollback: redirect routing to previous model variant and gracefully drain new nodes.

Operational run tasks & monitoring:
- Health checks: per-node GPU temperature, GPU memory pressure, kv-cache hit rate, per-model inference errors.
- Alerts: P50/P95/P99 latency slipped beyond thresholds, deployment failure, KMS auth errors, audit-sink lag > 5 minutes.
- Cost telemetry: token-level counters aggregated per-route, reported to AstraHealth billing repo.

Testing & validation (pre-cutover):
- Synthetic load: 3 levels (smoke, normal, burst) with realistic token distributions and prompt prefix caching enabled.
- Functional: FHIR connector smoke tests to ensure headers/payload redaction ordering correct.
- Security: KMS end-to-end test (encrypt/decrypt), HSM signing verification, penetration check of control-plane endpoints.

Open questions / decisions pending (priority ordered):
1) Model family and quantization target — AstraHealth preference for 8-bit or 4-bit quantization? If 4-bit required, we should validate quality regressions for triage prompts.
2) Air-gapped telemetry policy — acceptable to buffer telemetry locally and ship during maintenance windows, or must ship in real-time to SIEM?
3) KMS protocol — KMIP HSM vs cloud KMS BYOK? Technical team to confirm performance constraints of KMIP.
4) Network egress approvals — exact list of control-plane IPs and mTLS cert exchange steps from customer security.
5) Legal: required retention period for inference logs (AstraHealth legal to confirm).

Immediate next steps (owners & ETA):
- Confirm quantization requirement (AstraHealth infra team) — owner: Diego Alvarez — ETA: 2026-02-28.
- Produce offline-releasable bundle prototype for air-gapped site — owner: Rina Cho — ETA: 2026-03-07.
- Terraform module skeleton PR (networking + compute) with remote-state integration — owner: Samir Rao — GH-PR-1748 — ETA: 2026-02-26.
- Perf harness run in staging with 24-node config and synthetic traffic — owner: Elise Morgan — ETA: 2026-03-03.

Notes to self (work-in-progress style):
- Keep model artifacts immutable and tag by semantic version + build id; avoid using latest alias in terraform-managed resources.
- Look into cross-node NVMe caching to speed up cold-start for KV caches.
- Draft Confluence how-to for customers to rotate HSM keys and validate audit logs.

Appendix: quick cost ballpark (monthly, rough)
- H100 cluster (160 GPUs) amortized hardware + support: ~$400k–700k/month (varies by procurement/finance terms).
- A100 fallback pool (40 GPUs): ~$60k–120k/month.
- Network, storage, ops: ~$20k–40k/month.
- Note: final number depends heavily on procurement discounts, rack density, and whether customer uses existing hardware.

Document status: draft — feedback requested from AstraHealth infra/security teams and Redwood solutions engineering.
